channel.title: RoofPayback blog
channel.description: Daily articles on U.S. electricity prices and rooftop solar payback, built on EIA and PVWatts data.

item.title: Should You Wait for Cheaper Solar Panels?
item.description: Waiting for cheaper panels costs a year of savings each time. See payback at $2,500, $3,000 and $3,500 per kW in five states, with first-year savings.

item.title: Is Solar Worth It for a Small Home or Low Bill?
item.description: A 6,000 kWh home pays back in 7.6 years in California and 14.9 in Texas. See right-sized costs, savings, and who should skip solar.

item.title: Sun or Electricity Price: What Drives Solar Payback?
item.description: Alaska has the least sun yet pays back in 12.1 years, faster than Arizona's 13.9. State data shows why electricity price beats sunshine for payback.

item.title: Solar Payback Myths Checked Against State Numbers
item.description: Does solar pay off in five years, lose money when payback is long, or wear out first? State figures for one example home check four common claims.

item.title: Solar Quote Checklist: What to Verify Before You Sign
item.description: Check price per watt, yearly kWh and your utility's export credit before signing a solar quote. The cash median is $3.50 per watt; loans run $4.70.

item.title: How Much Electricity Does a Solar Panel Make Monthly?
item.description: A south-facing kW makes 1,755 kWh a year in Phoenix and 1,088 in Seattle. See output per panel and per month by state, and how to scale it to your system.

item.title: Is Solar Worth It in New York? The Payback Math
item.description: New York's high power prices drive solar payback, not sunshine. See 2026 price data, payback at full, half and quarter export credit, and how to check yours.

item.title: Is Solar Worth It Where Electricity Is Cheap?
item.description: Low electricity prices mean slower solar payback. See eight cheap-power states, how sun and export credits change the math, and how to check your own numbers.

item.title: Solar in Alaska vs. Hawaii: Which Pays Back Faster?
item.description: Alaska and Hawaii both have costly power. See how sunshine, prices and export credit change solar payback in each state, with side-by-side numbers.

item.title: Solar Panels in the South Central States: TX, OK, AR, LA
item.description: Texas, Oklahoma, Arkansas and Louisiana have decent sun but low power prices. See solar payback for each, and how export credit rules change it.

item.title: Solar Panels on the Pacific Coast: Three States Compared
item.description: Compare solar payback in California, Oregon and Washington using EIA prices and PVWatts output, and see why Northwest winters and cheap power stretch it.

item.title: Solar Panels in the Mid-Atlantic: Payback by State
item.description: How fast rooftop solar pays back in New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Delaware, Maryland and D.C., based on EIA prices and PVWatts output.

item.title: Is Solar Worth It in the Midwest? State-by-State Payback
item.description: Midwest solar payback depends more on your electric rate than on sunshine. Compare twelve states using August 2026 EIA prices and PVWatts output.

item.title: Solar Payback in the Southeast: Sun Meets Cheap Power
item.description: Southeast solar paybacks run from 14.1 to 17.6 years in our example. See why cheap power, not sunshine, sets the pace in eight Southern states.

item.title: Why Is Electricity So Expensive in Hawaii? EIA Data
item.description: Hawaii pays 47.18¢ per kWh versus 18.16¢ nationally, mainly because it burns imported petroleum. See the EIA data, how fast prices rose, and what it means.

item.title: Can You Choose Your Electricity Supplier? States Explained
item.description: Some states let you pick your electricity supplier. Learn how retail choice works and how to compare a supplier's price per kWh with the EIA state average.

item.title: Solar Panels in the Mountain West: Payback by State
item.description: Solar output, power prices and example payback in eight Mountain West states, from Wyoming and Idaho to Colorado and Arizona, and why cheap power slows it.

item.title: Solar Panels in New England: Prices, Sun and Payback
item.description: Maine, New Hampshire, Massachusetts and more: how high New England electricity prices and lower winter sun shape solar payback for an example home.

item.title: Is Solar Worth It in Texas? Cost and Payback
item.description: How much do solar panels cost in Texas, and how long until they pay back? See Houston payback by price per watt and export credit, with clear assumptions.

item.title: Is Solar Worth It in California in 2026?
item.description: California solar payback in our example home: 7.4 years with full export credit, 9.8 with half, 12.5 with quarter. See how credit rules change the answer.

item.title: Is Solar Worth It in Cloudy States? What the Numbers Show
item.description: Cloudy states can still see solar pay off when electricity prices are high. See output, prices and payback for the lowest-sunshine states.

item.title: Solar Panels for an Electric Car: How Much Bigger?
item.description: Adding an EV means more kWh per year. See how right-sized solar systems and payback change in four example states, with assumptions stated.

item.title: Solar for High-Usage Homes: Does a Bigger Bill Pay Back Faster?
item.description: Does a high electric bill mean faster solar payback? We compare small, average and large homes in TX, CA, FL and AZ with right-sized systems.

item.title: Solar Panel Degradation: 0.5% vs 0.8% Over 25 Years
item.description: How much output do solar panels lose over 25 years? Compare 0.5% and 0.8% yearly degradation and see the effect on payback and savings in five states.

item.title: Solar Payback If Electricity Prices Keep Rising
item.description: See how 0%, 2.5% and 4% yearly electricity price growth change solar payback and 25-year gain for an example home in five states.

item.title: Daytime Power Use and Solar Payback: 30%, 40%, 60%
item.description: How using more solar power during the day changes payback under full and reduced export credits, with results for California, Texas, Florida and Arizona.

item.title: Electricity Prices in August 2026: Where They Rose and Fell
item.description: U.S. home electricity averaged 18.16¢/kWh in August 2026, up 3.4%. See which states rose or fell most, how July compared, and what it means for bills.

item.title: Solar Loan vs. Cash: How Financing Changes Payback
item.description: Loan-financed solar had a higher median installed price than cash in Berkeley Lab data. See how interest changes payback and when savings cover payments.

item.title: Solar Panel Cost Per Watt and Payback by State
item.description: What a solar quote's price per watt means for payback in your state: national installed-price ranges, a three-quote example and the numbers to check first.

item.title: How to Lower Your Electric Bill: Steps That Add Up
item.description: Practical ways to lower your electric bill, with what one saved kWh is worth in each state and when rate plans or solar make sense.
